The biggest misread of anyone predicting the end of software engineering was imagining that the world only needed a certain amount of software, and bringing automation to the field would reduce the need for labor. 

Exactly the opposite is happening where essentially most things are actually turning into software. Because agents can use tools, work with computers, write software on the fly, and process data like humans (but far faster), we can now throw “software” at problems that never could reasonably be digitized before.

What that leads to is the role of engineering taking on greater importance in the economy, because we can now engineer far more systems and processes than were possible before.

If you’re a bank trying to do new forms of trading, engineers are often your first bet. If you are in life sciences, you expect more and more research and lab work to be engineering centric. If you’re in manufacturing, you’re trying to automate more of the supply chain, all that is engineering. More and more work is shaped like software problems.

Yes we’re not going to be coding manually in the future. But almost everything will be code, which means those that understand it are in a fantastic position.

It’s incredible to have reached a threshold where it’s practical that AI will be better at training models than humans are so quickly. One day recursive self improvement feels far off, and the next we already have signs of what it will look like.

Model capability finally exceeding most human engineers, advancements in the harness and infra for long running agents, a growing array of data, and the ability to parallelize the agents to work on vastly more tasks and tests and approaches than any person could have before, creates an incredible flywheel. 

This flywheel will almost certainly accelerate model progress far faster than we’ve seen before - or at a minimum enable pushing up the ceiling of the frontier at an insane rate. If you aren’t pricing in what RSI will lead to, that’s probably a mistake.

We tracked the best agent from @AnthropicAI, @OpenAI, @GoogleDeepMind, @Kimi_Moonshot, @SpaceXSI and @deepseek_ai across 4 key Agent Arena signals used between late June and the start of October to see how the industry is shifting.

Three things stood out:
1. Users like some agents far more than others.

On Praise vs Complaint, OpenAI and Anthropic sit at +35 points over the leaderboard average. Moonshot, xAI and DeepSeek land between +5 and +13. No other signal splits the labs this widely.

2. Agents are getting much better at delivery.

On Confirmed Success, the average lab's best model went from -4 to +14 points in three months. Anthropic leads with Claude Opus 5.5 (Max) at +20.

3. Labs are converging on error recovery and steering.

Since June, the spread between the six labs has more than halved on Bash Recovery (34 → 16 points) and nearly halved on Steerability (19 → 11).

In short, the labs are catching up on avoiding failures.

Leaving the user happy is where the top three are pulling away.

Liquid AI has released d1-ultra, taking the #1 position on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v1.0, supported by a reduction in hallucinations

d1-ultra is the new decision model from @liquidai and follows on from their release of d1 earlier this month. It is priced at $0.042 per 1M input tokens compared to $0.02 per 1M input tokens for d1. Like d1, d1-ultra is billed only on input tokens.

Key takeaways:

➤ d1-ultra leads the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v1.0 with a score of 65: d1-ultra scores 65, ahead of the recently released Jev 1.14 at 57 and GLiDE and Microsoft-Decision-1 at 54

➤ d1-ultra’s score of 65 is driven by a much lower hallucination rate on AA-Omniscience-Decision: d1-ultra’s non-hallucination rate on AA-Omniscience-Decision is 85%, up substantially compared to d1 at 2%. The non-hallucination rate is the share of questions not answered correctly where the model chose "I don't know" and measures how well a decision model can judge its own knowledge in knowing when not to answer. While d1-ultra’s hallucination rate decreases, so does its accuracy (% questions correct). It achieves an accuracy of 32%, down 9 points compared to d1 (41%)

➤ d1-ultra has the third lowest Time per Task of any decision model: d1-ultra achieves a Time per Task of 92 ms, the third lowest of decision models measured, behind Jev 1.14 at 78 ms per task and Celeris-1 Decision at 63 ms per task

➤ d1-ultra offers comparable pricing to other decision models at $32 per 1M tasks: At $32 per 1M tasks, d1-ultra is comparably priced to Celeris-1 Decision ($32 per 1M tasks) and Microsoft-Decision-1 ($31 per 1M tasks), more than double the price of d1 and Mercury Decide at $15 per 1M tasks but less than half the price of GPT-6 Luna (Decisions) at $79 per 1M tasks

Reflection’s first model, Beam, scores 30 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, placing it #2 among US open weights models

Beam is an open weights model with 501B total and 23B active parameters, released on @huggingface 

Congratulations to @reflection_ai on the release!

Key takeaways:

➤ Second among US open weights models: Beam scores 30, behind only Meta's Muse Spark Open (39) and ahead of yesterday’s NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL (26) release. Outside China, only Muse Spark Open and the UAE's K2 Horizon (31) score higher

➤ Token efficient for its intelligence: Beam uses ~26k output tokens per Intelligence Index task compared to K2 Horizon, one point ahead, which uses twice as many (~52k). Proprietary models still set the frontier, with GPT-6 Astra (max) scoring 53 on the same budget (~27k)

➤ Strong on agentic workflows, weaker in the terminal: Beam scores 48.5% on AutomationBench-AA, 11 percentage points ahead of K2 Horizon (37.2%) and level with Qwen3.8 27B (48.2%). Terminal-Bench 4.0 is a weak point, where Beam scores 3.0%, behind Qwen3.8 27B (5.6%) and Muse Spark Open (8.1%)

➤ Knows more, guesses more: On AA-Omniscience it answers 33% of questions correctly, well ahead of K2 Horizon (18%) and Qwen3.8 27B (16%). But its hallucination rate is 47%, against 26% for K2 Horizon and 30% for Qwen3.8 27B, giving Beam a net index score of 1.5, ahead of both peers (−3.0 and −10.0)

Other model details
Context window: 1M tokens
Modalities: Text
Parameters: 501B / 23B

Initial results for NVIDIA's Vera Rubin NVL72 are now live on AA-AgentPerf, with up to ~5.7x the total throughput per megawatt of its predecessor GB300 NVL72 on DeepSeek V4 Pro, ~5.4x on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, ~3.0x on GLM-5.2 and ~2.8x on Kimi K3

Vera Rubin is NVIDIA's successor to Blackwell, and Vera Rubin NVL72 is its rack-scale system, with 72 Rubin GPUs and 36 Vera CPUs. Each Rubin GPU has the same 288 GB of memory as Blackwell Ultra, but 2.4x the memory bandwidth, 1.7x the NVLink bandwidth and 2.3x the dense NVFP4 compute. NVIDIA submitted every Vera Rubin result, running TensorRT-LLM and vLLM with NVIDIA Dynamo

AA-AgentPerf is our agentic inference performance benchmark. It replays real agentic coding sessions, including long cached contexts and tool-call delays, to give a realistic measure of inference performance in day-to-day agentic workloads. We measure total system throughput per megawatt of measured GPU power, and per-agent output speed (p25 across requests) at varying concurrency levels, to show the trade-off between system utilization and individual user experience

Initial results:

➤ Vera Rubin's lead is largest at faster per-user speeds, where GB300's throughput falls away. On DeepSeek V4 Pro, going from ~120 to ~165 tok/s per user costs GB300 81% of its throughput per MW, compared to 16% for Vera Rubin

➤ At peak throughput the two are closer, with Vera Rubin at 272M tokens/s per MW on DeepSeek V4 Pro vs 239M for GB300 (1.14x), 571M vs 395M on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1.45x), 272M vs 201M on GLM-5.2 (1.35x) and 70M vs 56M on Kimi K3 (1.26x). We expect the gap between the systems to widen as Vera Rubin kernels and other serving software are optimized

➤ Vera Rubin sets the fastest per-user speeds on our leaderboard for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (906 tok/s, the fastest result for any model), GLM-5.2 (408 tok/s) and Kimi K3 (255 tok/s)

Congratulations @nvidia on the strong results!

In the bald and barren north, there is a dark sea, the Lake of Heaven. In it is a fish which is several thousand li across, and no one knows how long. His name is K’un. There is also a bird there, named P’eng, with a back like Mount T’ai and wings like clouds filling the sky. He beats the whirlwind, leaps into the air, and rises up ninety thousand li, cutting through the clouds and mist, shouldering the blue sky, and then he turns his eyes south and prepares to journey to the southern darkness.

The little quail laughs at him, saying, ‘Where does he think he’s going? I give a great leap and fly up, but I never get more than ten or twelve yards before I come down fluttering among the weeds and brambles. And that’s the best kind of flying anyway! Where does he think he’s going?’

Such is the difference between big and little.

part 3 of "software is taking off"

there's a profound misconception that led to people saying "software is dead": they think software = code

if software = code, and anyone's agent can write said code as needed, then of course it'll be hard to sell software

but most of the valuable software we use today is not just a pile of code!

good software is often the glue behind a network. your agent can vibe code a clone of X, instagram, uber all you want - but you won't even use it yourself, because the people you care about aren't there

good software is often the tip of an infrastructure iceberg. can your agent vibe code google on the fly? even if it wrote the code, where do you get the billion-dollar data centers to run the code?

good software is often a business model. want to vibe code a tinder clone? even if we ignore the network effect which your agent has absolutely no way to replicate, you still have to figure out - how on earth are you going to afford all the servers? 

if you charge every user, you instantly kill the network. if you let people use it for free, you bankrupt yourself. it took a lot of effort to find the delicate balance between who would pay, for what features, and by how much

good software is often also its compliance. do you honestly think companies buy salesforce and workday etc because they have beautiful high quality code that no one else can write? i mean.. have you looked at those products? 

but if you let your agents vibe code a clone, you immediately get into a rabbit hole of questions like - where do you store which piece of your data? how long can you keep them? what laws and regulations in each country just changed that require your vibe coded clone to keep up? one little mistake, and you get a very costly lawsuit

companies pay for those saas because they want someone else to take care of those complexity, so they can focus on their actual business, not spending their own time and take legal risks on their own shoulders

good software is often a lot of negotiations. want to vibe code spotify? well, first hire a big law firm and good luck negotiating all the licensing and rev share agreements

i can keep going on and on, but i think what i wrote above already gives a clear idea that valuable software is not just code, and cannot be replaced by an agent replicating its implementation

now, i should also point out that some software today is indeed just a small pile of code, like a fitness tracker. simple client-only applications may be what some indie hackers were counting on, but they would likely not carry a sustainable business, even today. that's never been what defines the software industry

i also think it's a profound mistake if people use AI only to repeat what already exists. i think the majority of the value AI brings will come from achieving things that weren't quite possible before. and i'll talk more about that in a subsequent part of this series
